analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 18 percent, including all fees.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap credit card rates at 18% never left the Senate Banking Committee and ended with the Congress in January 2025, without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended a federal consumer credit law to make it illegal for credit card companies to charge more than 18% annual interest, with all finance charges counted toward that limit. It also barred companies from piling on fees to get around the cap and allowed borrowers to sue companies that broke it. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly half of American cardholders who carry a balance month to month. Many standard credit card rates run above 20%, so the cap would have directly lowered interest charges for people who revolve debt, and the anti-evasion provision would have stopped companies from renaming interest as fees.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card borrowing at 18 percentage points, counting every finance charge toward that limit.

Prohibits fees that are not counted as finance charges from being used to evade the cap, and caps the total of such fees at the total of finance charges, so companies cannot disguise interest as junk fees.
Makes violating creditors subject to civil liability under the Truth in Lending Act's enforcement provisions, letting borrowers take legal action.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — major banks and card companies — would bear the cost, giving up interest and fee revenue on the portion of balances now charged above 18%. Cardholders with the weakest credit could also pay in a different way: issuers facing a hard cap might cut credit lines or stop lending to the riskiest borrowers rather than lend at 18%.

drawbacks.text: A hard 18% cap can price out borrowers with poor credit: issuers who cannot charge a rate that matches the risk may deny them cards or lower their limits, pushing some toward worse alternatives like payday loans. This is the standard objection to any interest rate cap and an honest supporter must weigh it.
The bill contains no offsetting provisions — no expanded alternatives for borrowers with poor credit — so the entire adjustment would fall on the least creditworthy consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the majority of cardholders who carry balances at rates above 18%, the benefit is direct and immediate: lower interest bills, with fee evasion expressly closed off. The real cost falls on borrowers with the worst credit, who might lose access to mainstream cards under a hard cap. The bill did nothing to address that trade-off, and it never advanced far enough for the argument to be tested in a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee the same day and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the Capping Credit Card Interest Rates Act on September 11, 2023.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the day it was introduced; that was the last action of any kind.
No senator cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor list shows zero.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still in committee, so it died without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers are better off, because the 18% cap never came close to a vote and the existing structure — rates that commonly exceed 20% plus layered fees — stayed intact through the entire Congress. Cardholders who carry balances got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers; no rate cap

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap credit card interest rates at 18% and referred it to the Banking Committee.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's only action was the referral itself.

against.name: Credit card industry
against.role: Issuers whose revenue depends on rates above the proposed cap
against.what_they_did: Opposed interest rate caps and defended the existing pricing structure during the period the bill was pending.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no senator from either party signed on, so the bill's support stayed at one Republican sponsor and there is no record of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (major banks and card companies)
industries.note: Issuers commonly charge rates above 20% on balances; a hard 18% cap covering all finance charges, with fee-evasion barred, would directly cut the interest and fee revenue they collect from cardholders who revolve debt. Their interest ran against borrowers' savings in this bill.

industries.industry: Alternative high-cost lenders (payday and installment lenders)
industries.note: If a hard cap pushes issuers to cut off the riskiest borrowers, some of those consumers shift to products with far higher effective costs — a spillover the bill did not address.
